name: Ethyl ascorbic acid

lead: Ethyl ascorbic acid (3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid) is a modified vitamin C used in brightening and anti-aging skincare. People use it to chase an even, radiant complexion and fewer dull or dark patches.

It is described as a tyrosinase inhibitor, the enzyme behind melanin production, so less pigment forms and tone looks more even. Published work is mostly cell studies, animal-skin studies and formulation papers; in cultured cells it reduced melanin production and showed antioxidant effects in UV-exposed keratinocytes. No controlled human trials were found.

paras: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, commonly in a morning routine with sunscreen, sometimes alongside other brightening ingredients. Tone changes from pigment-targeting products are generally watched over weeks to months.
At least one case report documents allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics containing it. Systematic safety data are limited. People with reactive skin or known allergies may want to patch test.

chain: Inhibits tyrosinase as vitamin C form
angle.text: Ethyl ascorbic acid is a vitamin C derivative used in brightening serums for an even, radiant complexion. It inhibits tyrosinase, which means less melanin and a more even tone. Lab and cell studies support this mechanism.

lead: 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid (ethyl ascorbic acid, EAC) is an ether derivative of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-ageing skincare. It is described as a tyrosinase inhibitor and is widely used in formulations, although the mechanisms behind its effects have been described as poorly understood [1].

Evidence for it in people is sparse. The bulk of published work consists of cell and animal-skin studies, formulation and analysis papers, and at least one case report of allergic contact dermatitis [2].

paras: EAC is an ascorbic acid with an ethyl group on the 3-position, used in skincare formulations for pigment-lightening and antioxidant purposes [1]. Methods have been published to measure it in whitening creams alongside arbutin and niacinamide [3].

In a 2021 study, EAC reduced melanogenesis in cultured melanocytes and acted via Nrf2-mediated inhibition of alpha-MSH in UVA-irradiated keratinocytes, with autophagy induction in melanocytes [1]. Later in vitro work paired it with cannabigerol in UV-irradiated keratinocytes [4][5], and another compared antioxidants for protection of skin cells against UVA [6]. A mouse-skin study found laser pretreatment increased EAC permeation [7], and formulation research has examined liquid-crystal vehicles for skin retention [8].
A 2019 case report described allergic contact dermatitis from 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid in facial anti-ageing cosmetics [2].
No controlled clinical trials of EAC alone were found. Research is limited to in vitro, animal-skin, formulation and case-report literature [1][2][7].
